scenes.caption: Separate the direct addition from the later reaction.

voiceover.text: Imagine our mixture already at equilibrium. A becomes B while B becomes A at the same average rate. Now add a little more A. Does B rise at that instant too? We added A, not B. Extra B has to be made by reaction. Watch those two moments separately: what we change directly, then what the reaction does afterwards.

scenes.body: A ⇌ B. Brief addition, then close the mixture again.
scenes.callout: Extra B has to be made by reaction.

scenes.caption: Only A jumps. Reaction changes both concentrations afterwards.

voiceover.text: Keep the one-to-one A and B model, with temperature and volume fixed. Concentration means amount per volume. Briefly add A, then close the container again. Only A jumps up. In our model, each direction is faster when more of its starting substance is present. More A makes A to B faster. B has not changed yet, so B to A is initially unchanged. More B is now made than used. A falls from its jump while B rises. Their changing amounts bring the rates back towards equality. The original-level marks matter: A finishes below its immediate jump, but above its original level in this model. The reaction uses some of the extra A, rather than undoing our addition completely.

scenes.body: A ⇌ B. Fixed temperature and volume.

bullets.text: A ⇌ B. Fixed temperature and volume.

scenes.caption: Reset the experiment. Replacement is partial in this model.

voiceover.text: Reset to the original equilibrium for a separate experiment. Remove some B, then close the container again. B drops immediately. A does not jump. Less B slows B to A at first, so A to B is now faster. B starts recovering from its drop while A decreases. That is a shift towards B: the direction of the reaction after our change. In this model, B still finishes below its original level. A shift towards B does not mean B is higher than it was before we removed it.

scenes.body: A ⇌ B. Fixed temperature and volume; reclose.

bullets.text: A ⇌ B. Fixed temperature and volume; reclose.
B to A initially slower; A to B faster.
B partly recovers, but remains below original.

scenes.caption: Use the written heat-releasing direction to predict the response.

voiceover.text: Now change temperature instead, keeping matter inside and volume fixed. Two nitrogen dioxide molecules join to form one dinitrogen tetroxide molecule. Joining releases heat: we call that direction exothermic, meaning heat-releasing. Splitting absorbs heat. Heating favours the heat-absorbing direction in the new equilibrium, so there is more nitrogen dioxide and less dinitrogen tetroxide. Nitrogen dioxide is brown; dinitrogen tetroxide is colourless. The warmer mixture is therefore browner. Cooling favours the heat-releasing direction and gives the opposite result. First identify which direction releases heat. Heating does not always give more of the written product.

scenes.heading: Which direction releases heat?

bullets.text: Heating favours splitting; cooling favours joining.

scenes.caption: Temperature changes K; composition adjusts afterwards.

voiceover.text: Watch the concentration graph during an idealised rapid temperature change. We keep volume fixed and transfer no reacting material into or out of the container. So neither concentration jumps just because we heated it. The reaction changes the concentrations afterwards. Heating changes how readily the opposing reactions happen, and for this heat-releasing joining reaction their previous balance is lost in favour of splitting. Nitrogen dioxide rises while dinitrogen tetroxide falls. Hold the new temperature steady as the mixture approaches a new balance. The missing vertical jump is useful here because our stated change was temperature alone at fixed volume. It would not identify the cause of every unknown graph.

scenes.caption: Next: gaseous equilibria and volume.

voiceover.text: Le Chatelier’s principle summarises the response: a disturbed equilibrium reacts in a direction that opposes the imposed change. Our rate comparison explains how that response happens. A useful anchor is direct change first, reaction follows. For temperature, identify heat release before predicting the direction. Treat writing heat beside the equation as a memory aid, not as a literal concentration of heat. Next, we will change the volume of a gaseous equilibrium. Here are the useful notes. Pause to copy if you need longer.

Concentration change: At fixed temperature and volume, adding or removing a substance changes that concentration first.
Temperature change: Heating favours heat absorption; cooling favours heat release. Identify the written direction.
